lead: A three-phase supply is three sinusoids of equal RMS value and frequency, spaced 120° apart. At every instant their powers add to a constant, and in a balanced load their currents cancel in the neutral. That lets a balanced system be solved as one phase. An unbalanced load breaks the cancellation: the neutral point shifts, currents differ, and you must solve each phase and add phasors. It runs every 400 V motor and the grid itself.
prereq: You need: phasors for 120° shifts, impedance for per-phase Z, and single-phase power for cos φ.

sections.h3: Phase sequence, star and delta quantities

blocks.text: A three-phase source has three voltages of the same RMS value and frequency. Their phase angles are 0°, −120° and +120°. The order in which they reach their peaks is the phase sequence: R-Y-B means phase R peaks first, then Y 120° later, then B. Reverse two lines and the sequence becomes R-B-Y; motors then run backwards.
VL = √3 Vph and IL = Iph (star); VL = Vph and IL = √3 Iph (delta)

V<sub>ph</sub> is the RMS phase voltage across one branch; V<sub>L</sub> is the RMS line-to-line voltage; I<sub>ph</sub> is the RMS current inside one phase branch; I<sub>L</sub> is the RMS current in one line conductor.

In a star (wye) connection each phase sits between one line and the neutral, so V<sub>ph</sub> is line-to-neutral and V<sub>L</sub> is line-to-line. In a delta each phase sits between two lines, so V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>. A star source with its neutral wire brought out is a three-phase four-wire system; in Indian low-voltage supply that gives 400 V between lines and 230 V from line to neutral. Leave out the neutral and it is three-phase three-wire, and a delta is always three-wire.

For R-Y-B sequence the star line voltage V<sub>RY</sub> leads V<sub>R</sub> by 30° (see the figure), and in delta the line current I<sub>R</sub> lags the phase current I<sub>RY</sub> by 30°. The √3 goes with the larger line quantity: voltage in star, current in delta.
A balanced load has the same Z in every phase, so the three currents are equal and 120° apart; their sum, the neutral current of a four-wire star, is zero.

items: Identify the connection and write the per-phase impedance Z = R + jX.
Choose phase R. Find V<sub>ph</sub>: V<sub>L</sub>/√3 for star, V<sub>L</sub> for delta.
Find I<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>/Z and the angle φ = angle of Z. In star I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>; in delta I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>.
Find total real power P = 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ and reactive power Q = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> sin φ.

blocks.text: A balanced delta load can also be replaced by an equivalent star with Z<sub>star</sub> = Z<sub>delta</sub>/3 and solved the same way.

An unbalanced load has different Z in the three phases, or different phase angles. The currents no longer add to zero. In a four-wire star system with a solid neutral, each phase voltage is fixed by the supply, so each phase current is found on its own: I<sub>R</sub> = V<sub>R</sub>/Z<sub>R</sub>, I<sub>Y</sub> = V<sub>Y</sub>/Z<sub>Y</sub>, I<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>B</sub>/Z<sub>B</sub>. The neutral current is the phasor sum I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>. It is generally not zero.

V<sub>N′N</sub> is the shift of the load star point N′ from the source neutral N; V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>Y</sub>, V<sub>B</sub> are source phase voltages; Y<sub>R</sub> = 1/Z<sub>R</sub>, Y<sub>Y</sub> = 1/Z<sub>Y</sub>, Y<sub>B</sub> = 1/Z<sub>B</sub> are phase admittances.

Without a neutral, or with an impedance in it, the load star point N′ shifts. Find V<sub>N′N</sub> with the formula above (Millman's theorem); each load phase voltage is then V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>N′N</sub>, and so on.

A three-wire delta has no neutral. Each branch sits across a known line voltage, so each phase current is I<sub>RY</sub> = V<sub>RY</sub>/Z<sub>RY</sub> and so on; each line current is the difference of two phase currents, for example I<sub>R</sub> = I<sub>RY</sub> − I<sub>BR</sub>.

examples.question: A balanced star-connected load of Z = 10 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply. Find the phase current, line current, total real power and neutral current.
steps: Line voltage V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V. For star, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 = 400/1.732 = 230.9 V.
In star, line current I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub> = 19.8 A.
Total real power: P = 3 I<sub>ph</sub>² R = 3 × 19.8² × 10 = 11.76 kW. Check: √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = 1.732 × 400 × 19.8 × 0.857 = 11.76 kW.
The three currents are equal and 120° apart. Their phasor sum is zero, so neutral current I<sub>N</sub> = 0 A.
examples.answer: I<sub>ph</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> = 19.8 A, total real power P = 11.76 kW, neutral current I<sub>N</sub> = 0 A.
examples.check:
import math
VL = 400.0
Z = complex(10, 6)
Vph = VL / math.sqrt(3)
Zmag = abs(Z)
Iph = Vph / Zmag
phi = math.degrees(math.atan2(Z.imag, Z.real))
cosphi = math.cos(math.radians(phi))
P = 3 * Vph * Iph * cosphi
print(round(Iph, 1))
print(round(P / 1000, 2))
print(0.0)

examples.question: A 400 V, 50 Hz, R-Y-B (positive sequence) four-wire supply feeds a star-connected resistive load: Z<sub>R</sub> = 10 Ω, Z<sub>Y</sub> = 20 Ω, Z<sub>B</sub> = 20 Ω. (a) Find the line currents and the neutral current. (b) The neutral wire breaks. Find the shift of the load star point and the new load phase voltages and currents.
steps: (a) Phase voltages, V<sub>R</sub> as reference: V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 230.9 V, so V<sub>R</sub> = 230.9∠0°, V<sub>Y</sub> = 230.9∠−120°, V<sub>B</sub> = 230.9∠120° V.
With the neutral in place each phase sees its own supply voltage: I<sub>R</sub> = 230.9/10 = 23.09∠0° A, I<sub>Y</sub> = 230.9/20 = 11.55∠−120° A, I<sub>B</sub> = 11.55∠120° A.
Neutral current: I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>. The Y and B currents are equal and 120° apart, so their sum is 11.55∠180°. I<sub>N</sub> = 23.09 − 11.55 = 11.55∠0° A.

(b) Without the neutral, use the star-point formula with Y<sub>R</sub> = 0.1 S, Y<sub>Y</sub> = Y<sub>B</sub> = 0.05 S: V<sub>N′N</sub> = (230.9 × 0.1 + 230.9∠−120° × 0.05 + 230.9∠120° × 0.05)/0.2. The two 0.05 S terms add to 11.55∠180°, so V<sub>N′N</sub> = (23.09 − 11.55)/0.2 = 57.7∠0° V.

New load phase voltages: V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>N′N</sub> = 230.9 − 57.7 = 173.2 V; V<sub>Y</sub> − V<sub>N′N</sub> = (−115.5 − j200) − 57.7 = −173.2 − j200 V, that is 264.6∠−130.9° V; by symmetry the B phase has 264.6∠130.9° V.

New currents: I<sub>R</sub> = 173.2/10 = 17.32 A; I<sub>Y</sub> = 264.6/20 = 13.23∠−130.9° A = −8.66 − j10.0 A; I<sub>B</sub> = −8.66 + j10.0 A. Check: 17.32 − 8.66 − 8.66 = 0 and +j10 − j10 = 0, so the sum is zero as KCL needs.
examples.answer: (a) I<sub>R</sub> = 23.09 A, I<sub>Y</sub> = I<sub>B</sub> = 11.55 A, I<sub>N</sub> = 11.55∠0° A. (b) The star point shifts by 57.7 V; the heavily loaded R phase drops to 173.2 V while Y and B rise to 264.6 V, which is why a broken neutral burns out appliances on the lightly loaded phases. Total power falls from 10.67 kW to 10.0 kW.

traps: Using V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> for a delta load, or I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub> for a star load. The √3 belongs to line voltage in star and line current in delta.
Assuming the neutral current is zero after the load becomes unbalanced. It is zero only when the three phase currents are equal and 120° apart.
Forgetting the 30° shift between line and phase quantities in the phasor diagram: star line voltage leads phase voltage; delta line current lags phase current for R-Y-B sequence.
Applying the per-phase equivalent to an unbalanced star without a neutral. The neutral point shifts; find V<sub>N′N</sub> first.

quiz.a: The order in which the three phase voltages reach their positive peaks, such as R-Y-B: R first, then Y 120° later, then B.

quiz.q: Why is the neutral current zero in a balanced four-wire star system?
quiz.a: The three phase currents have equal RMS values and are 120° apart. Three equal phasors 120° apart add to zero, so their sum in the neutral is zero.

quiz.q: A balanced star load of Z = 8 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V line supply. Find the phase current and total real power.
The neutral wire of a four-wire star system opens while the load is unbalanced. What happens to the load phase voltages and the neutral current?
quiz.a: The open wire carries no current, so by KCL the three load currents must add to exactly zero and the load star point moves to a new voltage V<sub>N′N</sub>. The most heavily loaded phase gets less voltage and the others more; in the second worked example they rise from 230.9 V to 264.6 V.

quiz.q: A balanced delta load of Z = 30∠30° Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V line supply. Find the phase current and line current.
quiz.a: In delta V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V. I<sub>ph</sub> = 400/30 = 13.33 A. I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × 13.33 = 23.09 A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Unbalanced three-phase systems are studied with symmetrical components and load-flow programs, because neutral shift and negative-sequence current heat motors and trip relays. Search next: symmetrical components, neutral point displacement, negative-sequence protection.

figure.caption: Phasor diagram of the balanced star worked example. The phase voltages are 230.9 V, 120° apart; the line voltage V<sub>RY</sub> = V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>Y</sub> is √3 times longer and 30° ahead of V<sub>R</sub>. Each 19.8 A current lags its own phase voltage by 31°, and the three currents add to zero.
